after.text:
Before finishing a change, run `npm test` and `npm run lint`; both must pass.

## Conventions

- Keep zero dependencies. Use Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:test`, `node:assert/strict`) rather than adding packages.
- Use double quotes, semicolons, and named exports, matching existing files.
- Add a test in `test/count.test.js` for any change to counting or reading-time behavior.
- The default reading speed is 230 wpm, and it is set in two places: `readingMinutes` in `src/count.js` and the CLI fallback in `bin/mdtally.js`. Change both together.
- Reading time rounds up to whole minutes, with a minimum of 1. Tests assert this.

decision-doc.request: We have to pick how to do search for Driftwood. My messy notes are in search-notes.md. Write it up so Priya can make the call and the team can see why, save it under docs/.
decision-doc.summary: Turned messy notes into a decision doc recommending Postgres search, with two checks that could flip the call.
excerpt: Why Postgres: it's the only option that doesn't fail one of the team's hard constraints. Meilisearch would mean running a new service, which breaks "no new on-call." Algolia's ~$1,100/month is over the $500 limit, so it needs CFO sign-off.
Sort the 41 August search tickets into typo, ingredient, filter and other. If typo complaints are the biggest group, Meilisearch becomes the better choice.
Sam's case for Meilisearch is written up fairly as the main counterargument, alongside Maya's preference for Postgres.
decision-doc.caveat: Owners and due dates for the next steps are its own suggestions, flagged for checking.

before.label: Your notes
before.text:
Options we talked about:
1. Postgres full-text search (tsvector + GIN index, pg_trgm for typos). No new infra. Maya prototyped it in 2 days: p95 38ms on a prod snapshot. Typo tolerance with pg_trgm is "okay, not great". Faceted counts would need hand-written queries.
2. Meilisearch self-hosted. Great typo tolerance and facets out of the box. Need to run + monitor another service and build a sync pipeline from Postgres. Sam estimates 2 weeks to production-ready.
3. Algolia (hosted). Best relevance tooling, zero ops. Quote we got: about $1,100/month at our projected volume. Finance said anything over $500/month recurring needs CFO sign-off.

Constraints: launch the new search before the January "healthy eating" campaign (Jan 6). Nobody wants a new on-call rotation.

after.label: Decision record
after.text:
Build on Postgres full-text search (tsvector + GIN, with pg_trgm for typos), and start logging zero-result queries now. Look at it again in February with real query data. If typo misses or facet work turn out to be the bottleneck, move to Meilisearch or Algolia then.

Confidence: medium. It covers the must-haves (ingredient search, filters, the deadline, no new on-call) with the least risk. It is weakest on typo tolerance, and we don't yet know how much typo tolerance matters to users.

before.text:
Rough thoughts from the founder:
- Owner shares a folder by email invite. Invitees can view or edit.
- Edits should show up for everyone. We do NOT have real-time collaborative editing today; notes save on blur and last write wins.

after.label: Calls it made
after.text:
Calls I made:
- No copies. There's one real folder, and members get access to it. So "what happens to other people's copies" goes away: deleting the folder removes it for everyone. Support can restore it for 30 days, and members can copy any note into their own notes beforehand.
- No more "last write wins" for shared notes. Each save checks which version of the note it started from. If someone else saved in between, the later save becomes a "conflicted copy" next to the original, so no edit is ever lost. Silently losing someone's meeting notes would be the worst way this feature could fail.

after.label: Recommendation
after.text:
I'd hold off on the $2.5M seed in January. Fix your runway now, spend roughly November to March testing whether Harborline can grow into a venture-sized company, and decide in March. If the evidence is there, raise in Q2 from a stronger position. The full plan is in `raise-plan.md`.

Why not January:
- The market is small at today's price. Every independent US bike shop paying $99/month adds up to about $4.75M a year in revenue. With Canada and the UK it's about $7.7M, and that assumes you sign every shop. A seed investor needs a path to a much bigger company.
- You'd be raising with almost no cash left. At $28k/month burn you'd have about 4.5 months of money on January 1 and run out around May 2027. Rounds often take months, so you'd be negotiating against that deadline.

product-experiments.request: We ran the onboarding checklist test for two weeks. Results and notes are in results/. The PM wants to ship Monday because the numbers look up. Can we? Put your answer in results/readout.md.
product-experiments.summary: Read a two-week A/B result, found the arms were uneven by about 640 users, and advised against shipping Monday.
excerpt: My answer is no, don't ship Monday. The checklist arm does look better, but the test result isn't valid as it stands.

The arms are uneven. Assignment was meant to be 50/50, but control has 10,120 users and the checklist arm has 9,480. A gap that size is very unlikely to be chance (p ≈ 5×10⁻⁶). About 640 users are missing from the checklist arm.

The lift depends on those users. The primary metric (3 notes created by day 7) is up 2.0 percentage points: 37.0% vs 35.0%. If 35 or fewer of the 640 missing users would have reached 3 notes, the lift disappears.
product-experiments.caveat: It worked only from a two-row summary CSV, so the Sept 6 to 8 crash check is still open.

2. Filter out internal work

Drop any PR labeled `internal`, `chore`, `refactor`, or `test`. Also drop it when there are no labels and the title prefix or the files show it's one of those (for example, it only touches tests, CI, or build config). Drop pure docs, dependency bumps, and other tooling work too, unless the body describes a change customers will notice.

Judge by what changed, not by how exciting the title sounds. A refactor titled "New sync engine" is still a refactor. This exact mistake has happened before. When a PR's label and its content disagree, trust the label for exclusion and mention the conflict in your report.

after.label: Cost review
after.text:
I've written `cost-review.md`. September AI spend comes to $13,819. That's $0.29 per monthly active user, or $4.46 per Pro subscriber if the whole bill is charged to paying users. Revenue is $24,800, so AI cost is 56% of it.

Where the margin goes: mostly the free tier. Features free users get account for $10,511 (76% of spend). An average Pro user costs about $1.29/month against $8 of revenue, so Pro is profitable. The ~44,900 free users cost about $9,800/month with no revenue behind them. If free users double while Pro stays flat, AI cost reaches about 95% of revenue. That growth risk matters more than any model choice.

Hi Ritika,

Your Sep 29 post said Nestfold's top resident complaint this quarter is money between flatmates (the gas cylinder, the party), and that your team gets pulled in when it shouldn't. I also saw that the Community Ops Associate role includes mediating cost-sharing disputes.

I'm building Tallyroom to keep those arguments between the flatmates. Each flat logs who paid for what, sees a running balance, and gets the fewest payments needed to settle up. It works in INR.

To be upfront: we're pre-launch. 31 people in 2 test flats used it in September, and we haven't worked with a co-living operator yet. That's why I'm asking about a small pilot rather than a rollout.

Would you be open to a 20-minute call to see whether a pilot in one or two Nestfold properties makes sense? If someone else owns this, I'd be grateful if you could point me to them.
